title: How Euler Wrote Pi (3Blue1Brown Pi Day 2018)
hook: Opens with two animated characters screaming competing circle constants at each other, immediately dramatizing a dry notational dispute as a personality clash.

scenes.purpose: Frame the pi-vs-tau debate as already settled, then pivot to a more interesting historical question

on_screen.desc: Randolph pi-creature shouting '3.1415...' in angry speech bubble
Tau-creature shouting '6.2831...' in angry speech bubble
Rotating radius with live decimal tracking circumference fraction

scenes.transition: Creatures removed; bare circle diagram kept as evidence
scenes.narration_gist: Everyone knows the tau debate — I'm not here to rehash it, I want to talk about the historical moment pi became standard.

scenes.purpose: Introduce primary sources and the Switzerland correspondent as credibility anchor

on_screen.desc: Portrait photo of Euler (Handmann painting)
Euler manuscript image faded, green highlight bar over key line
Quote: 'Let π be the circumference of a circle whose radius = 1'

scenes.transition: Photos fade in over blank stage; quote materializes beneath image
scenes.narration_gist: Euler himself used pi to mean 6.28 — likely borrowing π as 'p for perimeter' — so who's the villain who locked in 3.14?

scenes.purpose: Reveal the villain is also Euler, subverting the hero/villain framing just established

on_screen.desc: Clear Euler portrait labeled 'Used 6.2831...' in green
Pixelated then revealed same Euler portrait labeled 'Used 3.1415...' in red

scenes.transition: Pixelated image dissolves to reveal identical face; villain label appears
scenes.narration_gist: The 1748 calculus book that spread π = 3.14 across Europe was also written by Euler.

scenes.purpose: Show the actual book page and its exact wording to ground the claim in evidence

on_screen.desc: Facsimile page of Euler's Introductio, left half of screen
Highlighted quote with 'semicircumference', '3.14159', and 'π' in green
Circle animating with decimal ticking to π value, then line unwrapping

scenes.transition: Book page held left; animated circle diagram builds on right beneath quote
scenes.narration_gist: At the start of Chapter 8 Euler writes the semicircumference of a unit circle and says 'for brevity I will write π.'

scenes.purpose: Extend the twist: Euler also used π for a quarter-turn, showing it was context-dependent like θ

on_screen.desc: Circle with radius swept to quarter turn, arc highlighted
Labels 'π/2' and 'τ/4' stacked near arc endpoint
Number plane with radius rotating through several angles, θ label tracking

scenes.transition: Quarter-circle diagram kept; number plane fades in alongside for analogy
scenes.narration_gist: Euler used π the way we use θ — as whichever circle constant was most convenient for the problem at hand, not a fixed standard.

scenes.purpose: Establish Euler's staggering output to explain why he didn't fixate on notation

on_screen.desc: Scrolling list of ten 'Euler's formula / Euler's theorem' entries in different fields
Euler portrait with thought bubble
Thought bubble containing Basel problem series, cross over pi-vs-tau question

scenes.transition: List fades; portrait with thought bubble replaces it
scenes.narration_gist: Euler wrote 800 pages of dense math per year — his mind was on solving problems, not debating which circle constant is fundamental.

scenes.purpose: Deliver the core lesson: context determines the right convention, not abstract principle

on_screen.desc: Pi-creature looking sassy beside competing formula pairs (sum = −1/12 vs. diverges, etc.)
Title 'Which is right?' above pairs of contradictory-seeming math statements
Pi-creature in shruggie pose as final pair appears

scenes.transition: Debate pairs stack upward as new ones fade in from below; pi-creature emotion shifts each time
scenes.narration_gist: Fixating on which convention is objectively correct misses the point — focus on specific problems, and the right framing will follow from context.

scenes.purpose: Close with a practical punchline that redirects from meta-debate to actual mathematics

on_screen.desc: Tau-creature angry, demanding June 28th celebration
Pi-creature responding with Wallis product formula for π/2
Title: 'Happy π day!'

scenes.transition: Tau's angry bubble replaced by pi's math question; tau shifts to pondering
scenes.narration_gist: Next time someone says we should celebrate on 6/28, see how fast you can change the subject to actual math.

lessons: Open with a character conflict to dramatize an abstract disagreement before a single equation appears.
Stage a twist by withholding the punchline identity until after the audience has committed to a hero/villain frame — then reveal both roles belong to the same person.
Anchor historical claims with a visible primary-source image held in one half of the screen while the interpretation builds in the other half.
Use a live animated diagram (rotating radius with tracking decimal) to make an abstract constant feel like a measurable quantity rather than a symbol.
Let a character's emotional state (pi-creature's shruggie, pondering, sassy) pace the philosophical argument so the viewer feels the shift in register, not just reads it.
End not with a summary slide but with a scene that models the desired behavior — redirect from meta-debate to an actual problem — so the lesson is enacted, not stated.
